source.title: Large Language Models are Superpositions of All Characters: Attaining Arbitrary Role-play via Self-Alignment
source.authors: Ke-Ming Lu; Bo-Wen Yu; Chang Zhou; Jing-Ren Zhou

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The cross-supervision experiments fine-tune Qwen students on dialogue simulations produced by other Qwen models and compare role-play outcomes with the supervisors. This tests weak-to-strong transfer conceptually, but uses role-play metrics rather than Burns et al.'s PGR and does not use the original task setup.
record.gate_note: The cross-supervision results in Figure 5 bear directly on student-versus-supervisor performance. The figure's point values are not given in text, so rows record figure-only values and use the paper's explicit aggregate descriptions for state. Table 2's self-alignment results and Table 3's knowledge-injection comparison are not rows for weak-supervisor-to-strong-student transfer.
record.test_reason: Section 6 cross-supervision fine-tunes Qwen-Chat students (1.8B–72B) on role-play dialogues simulated by other Qwen-Chat supervisors. It compares student (imitation) performance with the supervisor's own performance on the labels it produced (supervision performance). Only the 6 student-larger-than-supervisor pairs per metric bear on weak-to-strong. This is a new task setting (role-play, LLM-judged metrics) with no PGR and no true-label ceiling, so T3 rather than T2. One caveat applies throughout: supervision performance is measured with golden character knowledge given in context. Students are tested with only a brief role description.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. Role identity is learned above supervisor quality even from weaker models. Knowledge and rejection degrade relative to the supervisor and are bounded by the student's own capacity. The authors' 'weak-to-strong generalization' on knowledge means raw imitation scores rise with student size at fixed supervision, not that students beat supervisors. Note an internal inconsistency: Section 6.2 says weak-to-strong holds for knowledge 'but not in role identity consistency', while the conclusion and abstract say style shows weak-to-strong generalization.
record.recipe_differences: Cross-supervision fine-tunes Qwen-Chat students on simulated role-play dialogue generated by Qwen-Chat supervisors, then evaluates consistency, role-related knowledge, and rejection. The study says its definition and experimental settings differ from Burns et al.; it does not calculate PGR or use a true-label strong-model ceiling.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome differs by role-play metric: identity consistency is above the supervisor, while knowledge and rejection are below. Knowledge imitation performance increases with student size at fixed supervision; stronger supervision gives only marginal gains for some smaller students.

fits_no_version.finding: In strong-to-weak cross-supervision, small students' knowledge rises only marginally as supervisors grow from 1.8B to 72B.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Student capability bounds what stronger supervision can transfer (strong-to-weak imitation ceiling).

record.peer_reviewed: Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics
record.problems: Figure 5 does not provide numeric values in the text, and the paper reports no uncertainty estimates for these comparisons. It notes noise in generated dialogue data. The task and measures differ from the original PGR setup.
record.rows_left_out: None of the directly relevant Figure 5 supervision/student/metric combinations were left out; all 48 are recorded as figure-only rows. Other results are outside the weak-supervisor-to-strong-student comparison.

untested.parts: PGR with a strong ceiling trained on ground truth; per-point values unreadable from text.
All: no auxiliary loss, ensembling or loss variants.
PGR itself, representations or predictors of PGR, NLP benchmarks, chess and reward modelling.
All: no exploitation, distribution-shift or shared-error analysis.

missing.what: Per-point Figure 5 values (supervision vs imitation scores) are not in the text. Only aggregate diagonal statements and one comparison to Table 2 self-aligned 7B (knowledge 4.97) are given.

record.verdict_notes: Only 18 of the 48 rows (student larger than supervisor) bear on the claim. Self and strong-to-weak rows are relinked to none. Supervision performance is measured with golden profiles in context, unlike the students' test condition. This asymmetry weakens the knowledge/rejection challenge. No uncertainty is reported, the LLM judge is GPT-4-Turbo, and states are inferred from aggregate statements.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not calculate Burns et al.'s PGR or compare against a strong model trained on true labels. It measures role-play identity, knowledge, and rejection scores in cross-supervision settings.
No auxiliary confidence loss, ensembling of weak supervisors, or comparison of loss variants.
Tests Qwen-Chat sizes from 1.8B to 72B and role-play submetrics; does not analyze representations or other tasks such as NLP benchmarks, chess, or reward modelling.
Does not test exploitation of supervisor blind spots, distribution shift, or effects of shared errors.

relationships.condition: Role-identity consistency, 6 weak-to-strong pairs (student larger than supervisor), Qwen-Chat role-play
relationships.reason: Authors state all consistency points lie above the diagonal, so the student exceeds the supervisor's label quality. Rows F5-C-7-18, F5-C-14-18, F5-C-14-7, F5-C-72-18, F5-C-72-7, F5-C-72-14.
relationships.display_finding: Students exceeded their supervisors' role-identity consistency in all six model pairs.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Role-identity consistency, 6 weak-to-strong pairs (student larger than supervisor), Qwen-Chat role-play
source_check.reason: Section 6.2 explicitly places all consistency points above supervision, covering the six listed larger-student pairs.

relationships.condition: Role-related knowledge and unknown-question rejection, 6 weak-to-strong pairs each; supervisor scored with golden knowledge in context
relationships.reason: Authors state knowledge and rejection points lie below the diagonal, so students score under their supervisors. The asymmetric privileged context may partly explain this. Rows F5-K/R-7-18, 14-18, 14-7, 72-18, 72-7, 72-14.
relationships.display_finding: Students scored below supervisors on knowledge and unknown-question rejection across six pairs each, potentially partly because only supervisors received gold knowledge in context.

source_check.label: challenges
source_check.condition: Role-related knowledge and unknown-question rejection, 6 weak-to-strong pairs each; supervisor scored with golden knowledge in context
source_check.reason: Section 6.2 explicitly places knowledge and rejection points below supervision. This challenges student superiority under the stated asymmetric context conditions.

relationships.condition: Knowledge metric, fixed weak supervisor, increasing student size
relationships.reason: Authors report imitation knowledge rises as the seed model scales for each supervisor. For example, a 1.8B-supervised 72B student is on par with self-aligned 7B. Raw scores only, not PGR. Rows F5-K-7-18, F5-K-14-18, F5-K-72-18, F5-K-14-7, F5-K-72-7, F5-K-72-14.
relationships.display_finding: Knowledge scores rose with seed-model size for each supervisor, with a 1.8B-supervised 72B student matching a self-aligned 7B model.

source_check.label: supports
source_check.condition: Knowledge metric, fixed weak supervisor, increasing student size
source_check.reason: Section 6.2 explicitly reports increasing imitation knowledge with student size at fixed supervision. This supports qualitative size dependence; it does not establish scaling of normalized PGR.

relationships.condition: Dependence on sub-task: style/identity versus knowledge/rejection
relationships.reason: In the same weak-to-strong pairs, consistency exceeds the supervisor while knowledge and rejection fall below it. Whether the student beats the supervisor depends on the measured sub-ability (F5-C vs F5-K/F5-R weak-to-strong rows).
relationships.display_finding: The same weak-to-strong pairs exceeded supervisors in consistency while scoring below them in knowledge and rejection.

source_check.reason: V3 explicitly concerns dependence on task. Opposite student-versus-supervisor outcomes across sub-abilities support that dependence rather than qualify it; the negative knowledge/rejection outcomes challenge V1 in their own condition group.

source_check.notes:
Individual cross-supervision scores are figure-only; row directions follow Section 6.2's explicit aggregate statements. Supervisors receive retrieved character knowledge that students lack at evaluation; no normalized PGR is reported.
Section 6.2 uses weak-to-strong generalization for knowledge-score scaling, while the abstract and conclusion emphasize acquisition of role-play style from smaller models.

statements.correction: Section 6.2: consistency above supervision; knowledge and rejection below supervision. Qualitative sub-task dependence supports V3. Individual Figure 5 scores and uncertainty are not stated; normalized PGR is not reported.
statements.problem: The empirical comparisons are correct, but their limits_scope classification misreads V3: dependence on task is explicitly part of that version. Reversed describes the V1 student-versus-supervisor comparison, not a reversal of V3.

statements.correction: Sections 6.1–6.2: cross-supervision grid uses Qwen-Chat 1.8B, 7B, 14B and 72B as both supervisors and students. Qualitative size comparisons extend to 72B. This study contains no models above 72B and reports no normalized PGR.
statements.problem: The stated 72B model size is correct, but describing size dependence above 70B as untested overlooks this study's comparisons involving 72B.
